#10177. How to Migrate an Elementor Site to the WordPress Block Editor

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

***Author Bio: ***Fahad Raza is a WordPress developer and SEO consultant based in Sydney. He has built websites since 2005, worked in SEO for more than 18 years, and spent eight and a half years on the IKEA Australia and New Zealand website.

#10176. Xreal Aura Review: Android XR combined with lightweight glasses delivers a true next-gen spatial computing experience

If you can get past the $1,000+ price of entry, the Xreal Aura really ups the ante for low-impact spatial computing.

Powerful Computing Puck adds another form of input

Familiar Android XR interface+ Access to the vast Android ecosystem

Can be used with Macs, Windows, and SteamOS devices

$1,099 starting price might scare off potential customers

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

The world of augmented reality (AR) and extended reality (XR) glasses is really starting to get interesting. This is particularly true of so-called “self-contained” systems that don’t rely solely on your smartphone or tablet to deliver content. The Xreal Aura, which was co-developed with Google, is the latest in the Android XR field, and it’s quite an ambitious project.

Although the Aura looks somewhat similar to previous Xreal glasses that we’ve reviewed, the AR goes a step further with a dedicated puck powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite SoC, hand/finger tracking, and the ability to interface wirelessly with accessories like keyboards and gamepads. The Aura really promises the ability to leave your smartphone at home and serve as the only computing platform you need (with some caveats).

The Aura’s design is clearly an evolution of the Xreal One Series, but with a few key differences. You’ll find the main changes up front, where you’ll now find two forward-facing, high-precision tracking cameras mounted at the corners of the frame. These cameras are used to continually track your head position, giving you the best possible experience for 6 degrees of freedom tracking for your hands and fingers.

At the center of the frame, there is a fully integrated single high-resolution camera for capturing photos or video. This was previously a separate add-on module for Xreal One Series AR glasses. There’s a red LED that illuminates when you’re recording so that people around you are made well aware of what’s going on if they have objections.

Your primary focal point, however, will be looking through the lenses, which are augmented by dual Sony-manufactured micro-OLED displays. You get one micro-OLED display per eye, each offering 1920 x 1200 resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and maximum brightness of 1,050 nits. However, there’s a major upgrade in the field of view (FoV), as the Aura expands to 70 degrees, up from 57 degrees on the One Pro.

The Aura is available in two SKUs to support the interpupillary distance (IPD) of a wide range of people. The Medium SKU supports people with an IPD of 60 to 66 mm, while the Large SKU ranges from 66 mm to 72 mm.

Given that the Aura is the flagship of Xreal’s AR/XR glasses lineup, it comes with electrochromic dimming for the lenses, which can automatically adjust transparency levels, or you can manually make adjustments (there are five levels of transparency available).

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The arms of the Aura look nearly identical to the ones you find on members of the One Series glasses. On the bottom is a red button, which, when pressed, allows you to manually adjust the brightness levels of the Aura. Directly adjacent is a rocker that allows you to control the volume. There’s another button on the top of the right arm that, when pressed once, takes you to the home menu. Double-pressing the button brings up the capture menu for taking pictures or videos with the forward-facing camera.

Bose-tuned speakers are also built into the arms of the Aura and feature an open-ear design so that you can remain engaged with what’s happening in your environment.

Xreal takes a two-pronged approach to hardware with the Aura. At a base level, the Aura is powered by the X1S Spatial Coprocessor, which allows you to experience traditional AR functionality with smartphones, tablets, PCs, and Macs, as you would with previous Xreal glasses.

But the real magic happens with the Xreal Computing Puck, which is a separate device that connects to the Aura using a USB-C cable. The puck looks and feels like a slightly oversized smartphone, albeit without a display. In place of the display, you’ll find a large touch-sensitive surface that can be used to interface with the Android XR interface.

The puck is powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform, which delivers 48 TOPS of AI computing power. It comes in 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB SKUs — our review unit was spec’d with the former. The puck features a 4,455 mAh battery that powers the glasses, and it even incorporates a fingerprint reader for authentication purposes in Android XR. The puck also fully supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3; the latter of which is essential for supporting Bluetooth accessories.

The puck is quite beefy, measuring roughly 5.85 x 2.85 x 0.5 inches and weighing 9.3 ounces. I had no issue just slipping the puck into my pants pocket, but Xreal also includes a detachable clip if you want to attach it to your pants pocket or other clothing. The puck also features a cooling fan to keep temperatures in check. Indeed, the device can get warm to the touch (after all, it’s basically a powerful screenless smartphone with a 4,455 mAh battery) during use – which explains why Xreal includes the clip and probably doesn’t want you putting the puck in your pocket, like I was prone to do.

My Aura review unit also came with an Xreal Keyboard and an Xreal Game Controller. Both connect to the Aura using Bluetooth and were easily set up by pairing them within the Bluetooth menu under Settings.

The keyboard is battery-powered and is recharged using a USB-C port at the top (just above the F7 key). It’s a nifty design that neatly folds when not in use. Interestingly, I couldn’t find a way to “lock” the hinged part of the keyboard when it’s fully extended. Because of this, you can’t use the keyboard sitting on your lap with your legs spread slightly apart, as the keyboard will simply collapse and fall to the floor if you apply any kind of pressure. You’ll either need to put your legs together or place the keyboard on a desk or table, which isn’t exactly ideal if you like the more “freeing” aspect of using XR glasses.

With that said, the keyboard is a lifesaver when it comes to text entry, be it for entering web addresses, writing emails, or anything that requires frequent use of the keyboard. It sure beats waving your fingers around to input text.

The game controller features an Xbox-style layout with four face buttons for gaming, two thumbsticks, a D-pad, and a Google Gemini/Home button. There are two shoulder buttons at the top and two triggers (with modes to function as microswitch triggers or Hall Effect analog triggers). There are also two remappable macro buttons under the shoulder buttons and two additional macro buttons on the underside of the controller (which can be turned off with physical switches).

Not only does the controller feature built-in rumble, but it also incorporates a 6-axis gyroscope for aiming and finger controls and a 3.5mm headphone jack built into the bottom of the unit. But perhaps the most interesting feature is a magnetic faceplate that breaks into three pieces. The main piece covers the face buttons, D-pad, and thumbsticks. The other two pieces cover the hand grips. You can purchase separate pieces to customize the look of the controller if you wish.

I found the controller comfortable to use, with a nice textured plastic finish for your palms to rest on (the bottom of the controller features a similar texture, but has a rubber coating over the plastic for better grip). And although the controller is designed for Bluetooth use with the Aura, it does feature a USB-C port and a USB dongle for connecting it wirelessly to a PC.

Another nice touch is that Xreal includes a charging dock for the controller that plugs in with a lengthy USB-A to USB-C cable. The controller itself charges with four pogo pins mounted on top of the dock (or via USB-C if you prefer).

After removing the Aura from its retail box, I wanted to get into the action quickly and didn’t bother initially charging the puck. I used the included USB-C to USB-C cable to plug from the left arm of the Aura into the dedicated USB-C port on the bottom of the puck. Next, I pressed the power button on the puck, after which the glasses sprang to life and began the setup process.

The setup process first had me perform a few gestures with my fingers to properly set up the viewing window for my eyes. Then, the setup program walked me through pointing, pinch, and drag-and-drop gestures to navigate through the user interface. It was also during this time that I was able to set up my Wi-Fi connection and log in to my Google account. Since I’m an iOS user and rarely, if ever, use Android, I couldn’t speed up setup by logging in with a nearby Android device. So I had to log in to my Google account by pointing and pinching with my fingers to enter my email address and password using the on-screen virtual keyboard. It was a tedious process, but I was eventually able to finish once I completed two-step authentication on my iPhone.

After taking some time to get used to dragging and pinching through the Android XR interface using my fingers, the experience began to feel almost natural. I was able to pinch to open apps, have multiple apps open at once, and drag or resize windows in my viewing space on command.

I was able to access all the typical stock apps like Chrome, Gmail, and Google Photos, which, of course, carried over my favorites, emails, and photos/vidoes, respectively. I spent quite a bit of time going down memory lane, watching videos of my two sons when they were toddlers among the hundreds of videos I have stored in Google Photos. It was also great to be navigating around the UI or working in the app, then seeing a notification pop up telling me that an email had arrived. I would then pinch the notification with my fingers to open Gmail.

The possibilities of how you can use the Aura are almost endless, and you can even mix other computing devices into the formula. For example, I was able to plug a USB-C cable from my MacBook Air into the second USB-C port on the puck (that’s usually reserved for recharging the puck). In an instant, my MacBook Air’s display was mirrored onto the glasses in front of me. So I could have Google Docs open as I typed, while having the Android XR native Gmail and YouTube apps flanking the virtual MacBook Air display.

It’s a similar experience with handheld gaming consoles. I was successfully able to connect a Lenovo Legion Go S (SteamOS) and an MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Windows 11) to the Aura glasses without issue, enjoying a vast library of games in fully immersive glory.

The native gaming experience isn’t bad either; I loaded up games like Fortnite and spent an hour toiling around in Grand Theft Auto III for a nostalgic treat ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The Xreal Game Controller made playing these games a breeze.

But I also used the Aura glasses for more mundane tasks. I was able to walk around the house, performing my usual chores, with a shrunken YouTube window playing videos in the top right corner of my field of view. True multitasking is at hand, folks.

I should note that open-air speakers sounded good, but not great. They sounded similar to the Bose-tuned speakers in the older Xreal One Pro. There's a good level of bass, and overall clarity is good. However, if you want a more immersive audio experience, the design of the Aura allows you to easily throw on a pair of headphones or wireless earbuds to compensate for any audio shortcomings.

The Xrea Aura is a true workhorse when it comes to spatial computing. By putting the bulk of the computing hardware into a smartphone-shaped Computing Puck, you have a low-impact way of experiencing XR without the hassle of wearing a bulky headset.

You can navigate the user interface using your hands, or the touch service of the puck. And for more specialized tasks, Xreal offers its own-branded keyboard and gamepad accessories (although you are free to use your own Bluetooth-enabled accessories).

Not only do you have access to the vast Android app ecosystem, but you can also connect to devices running Windows, macOS, or even SteamOS.

There’s a lot going on with this device, and there are limitless possibilities for how you could use the Aura. The only problem is that most people don’t have limitless funds, so the $1,099 price tag of our review unit (12GB RAM, 256GB of storage) is sure to give many people pause. Stepping up to 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage takes the price to $1,299. If you add in the Xreal Keyboard and Xreal Game Controller, the total cost of our review unit comes in at $1,277 ($1,477 for the 16GB/512GB configuration).

That’s a lot to ask for what is essentially a niche device. However, if you want a truly immersive XR experience that is not weighed down by geeky-looking headsets, it’s hard to argue with what Xreal is offering with the Aura.

#10175. Secure cloud storage is the cheaper, safer alternative to keeping files physical

Physical storage and memory are only getting more expensive, but that doesn’t mean we need to store any less. The alternative solution is a secure cloud storage platform, and there’s really only one good option.

That extends throughout every platform it’s available on, including Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux. On just about any platform, users get access to the pCloud Drive app for dedicated storage and backup. On Android and iOS, you have an additional option to automatically back up photos to free up space on your phone. pCloud Photos also acts as a smart photo gallery within the app, and sharing between other pCloud users and friends is made incredibly simple.

No matter where you access your pCloud Drive, all your files are there – safe and secure. You can store all kinds of files in pCloud, including documents, photos, videos, and even documents containing passwords.

Of course, you also get the option to take security a step further with pCloud Encryption. Your most sensitive files can be stored with an added layer of client-side, zero-knowledge encryption. The key is all yours, and no one else’s.

Even if you already have a hefty backup solution like an in-home NAS, pCloud is still a good option because it makes that NAS that much more useful. It has an official NAS backup feature with support for WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP. pCloud simply provides another safety net for your existing backup.

Unlike a lot of cloud storage services, pCloud doesn’t charge on a monthly or even yearly basis. Just like buying physical storage, paying once for what you need is enough. But what makes it a better option than going the traditional route – beyond the skyrocketing storage prices – is the features and security that come with it.

This just so happens to be the best time to choose secure cloud storage, too. pCloud’s Black Friday promotion runs from November 13 to November 28. Starting with the base 500GB lifetime storage plan, pCloud’s one-time price comes down to $159 – 43% off. The 2 TB plan is currently down to $379, while the massive 10GB lifetime plan is 61% off at $1,099. pCloud is also offering a bundled 3-in-1 option that includes 3TB of storage, a lifetime pCloud Pass subscription, and pCloud Encryption for $579.

Secure cloud storage has major advantages, and a one-time subscription for terabytes of storage is rare these days.

#10174. One-Shot Any Web App with Gradio's gr.HTML

Gradio 6 quietly shipped a very powerful feature: gr.HTML now supports custom templates, scoped CSS, and JavaScript interactivity. Which means you can build pretty much any web component — and Claude (or any other frontier LLM) can generate the whole thing in one shot: frontend, backend, and state management, all in a single Python file.

We tested this by building different types of apps. Each one is a single Python file, no build step, deployable to Hugging Face Spaces in seconds.

Pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

The tree animation alone would normally require a separate React component. Here it's just CSS keyframes in css_template and state updates in js_on_load.

GitHub Contribution Heatmap: Click any cell to toggle contributions. Multiple color themes. Pattern generators (streaks, seasonal, random). Live stats that update as you edit.

Kanban Board: Full drag-and-drop between columns. Inline editing (double-click any card). Search feature that can filter in real-time. Collapsible columns.

Drag-and-drop usually means pulling in a library. Here it's native HTML5 drag events wired up in js_on_load, with state synced back to Python via trigger('change').

Spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The community's built some creative components with gr.HTML too:

3D Camera Control for Image Editing: A full Three.js viewport inside a Gradio app! Drag handles to control azimuth, elevation, and distance. Your uploaded image appears in the 3D scene, and the camera parameters feed directly into Qwen's latest image editing model. These kinds of interactive 3D controls would normally require a separate frontend — with Gradio it's just one gr.HTML subclass🔥

Real-time Speech Transcription: Live transcription with Mistral's Voxtral model. The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

Every gr.HTML component takes three templates:

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

For reusable components, subclass gr.HTML:

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

When you ask your LLM to build a custom component, single-file output is everything. No "now create the styles file" or "wire this into your build config." Just one Python file that runs immediately.

The feedback loop becomes: describe what you want → get code → gradio app.py → see it working → describe what to fix → repeat. Each cycle takes seconds with Gradio's reload mode.

Deploy to Spaces with gradio deploy or share a temporary link with demo.launch(share=True). Within a few seconds from an idea to a live app.

Gradio ships with 32 interactive components, but sometimes your perfect AI web app needs something special. That's where gr.HTML comes in.

If you’ve got an idea, try building it with gr.HTML: describe what you want to your LLM, generate the code, run it. You might be surprised what you can ship in 5 minutes.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1, with an Nvidia lawyer following him on December 2, it's been confirmed. CNBC reports that the leaders of those panels broke the news today after days of speculation. Huang was asked to appear via a letter issued on November 9, just 24 hours after he admitted the affair with Alice Huang, a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy. Days later, it was also suggested that Mr. Huang could be issued a subpoena if he did not respond by tomorrow, November 18. That subpoena will no longer be required.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Rick Crawford, R-Ark., the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees, reportedly said after the news of the pair's December appearances was announced. "The American people need answers," they went on, noting that it would be "dangerous" to allow Chinese state actors access to advanced AI chips, the likes of which are built by Nvidia.

Ms. Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a company that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr. Huang's tenure as CEO. Megaspeed was later added to Nvidia's no-sell list following concerns that it was involved in the smuggling of AI chips to China against U.S. export laws. Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary, has been accused of importing Nvidia chips and then re-exporting them to China. A criminal investigation has since been launched into Megaspeed in an attempt to get to the bottom of the complicated web of AI companies and chip shipments.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia following his admission of an affair with Ms. Huang. Since then, reports of at least one other affair with an Nvidia employee have surfaced. Despite that fact, calls for Huang's return to the top job at Nvidia continue to gain momentum.

#10172. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training

Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

#10171. IBM and UC Berkeley Diagnose Why Enterprise Agents Fail Using IT-Bench and MAST

Ayhan Sebin Saurabh Jha Rohan Arora Daby Sow Mert Cemri Melissa Pan Ion Stoica

ITBench HF Space ITBench HF Dataset MAST HF Dataset ITBench Github MAST Github

IBM Research and UC Berkeley collaborated to study how agentic LLM systems break in real-world IT automation, for tasks involving incident triage, logs/metrics queries, and Kubernetes actions in long-horizon tool loops.

Benchmarks typically reduce performance to a single number, telling you whether an agent failed but never why. To solve this black-box problem, we applied MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), an emerging practice for diagnosing agentic reliability ). By leveraging MAST to analyze ITBench—the industry benchmark for SRE, Security, and FinOps automation—we turned raw execution traces into structured failure signatures, revealing exactly what broke and how to fix it. We annotated 310 ITBench SRE traces across three distinct model classes: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Takeaways from our analysis when building agents:

If you’re building agents for enterprise IT workflows, this is the kind of evaluation you want: not just “did it pass?”, but “what broke, where, and what intervention is most leverageable?”

Benchmarks like ITBench are becoming the standard for measuring agentic performance in high-stakes IT automation tasks. In ITBench, agents act as Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) or Security Analysts tasked with diagnosing Kubernetes outages, patching vulnerabilities, or managing cloud costs in production environments.

This benchmarks use success rate as a main metric to evaluate agents. However, this metric is insufficient for engineering robust systems. Knowing that an agentic system achieves a 14% success rate on ITBench tells us that it failed, but not why: Did it fail because it forgot the context? Because it hallucinated a command? Or because it simply did not terminate?

Without a comprehensive approach to diagnose these failures, developers are left guessing, often resorting to blind prompting tweaks that solve one problem only to create another.

As a new standard to analyze the failure modes of complex agentic systems, we developed MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy). MAST brings more insights and open up the opaque evaluation of these benchmarks. Derived from a rigorous analysis of over 1,600 traces across seven different frameworks, MAST provides a standardized taxonomy for agent failures.

MAST converts unstructured execution logs into structured "failure vectors" based on 14 distinct patterns across three key categories:

We stress-test the idea of using MAST to make agent evaluations actionable and gain insights on the failure modes by applying it to ITBench, a popular evaluation suite for IT automation tasks across SRE, Security/Compliance, and FinOps.

We annotated 310 ITBench SRE execution traces produced by an SRE agent built with Codex in realistic environments. These traces capture natural language interactions between agents and their tools across three models representing different capability tiers: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B. This lets us look past simple success metrics and investigate the distinct failure signatures driving these results. For this we use the recall scores, as the models by design only output a maximum of 3-5 outputs and SREs prefer the recall scores over F-1 score.

Below, we detail the findings from this diagnostic analysis.

When we examine the failed traces, a clear hierarchy of complexity becomes apparent across the three models. This is measured by the number of distinct failure modes observed per failed run.

This disparity in failure mode density reveals a fundamental difference in how these systems break down. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a surgical failure profile. Even in unsuccessful runs, it maintains high internal coherence and typically fails due to a single isolated failure, such as an incorrect verification step. These failures are precise and far easier to diagnose.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, GPT-OSS-120B suffers from cascading collapse. In these traces, we observe that errors tend to compound over time. A small reasoning mismatch early in the process often leads to a deviation from the task specification, which in turn triggers a total derailment of the agent. Kimi-K2 represents the middle ground, where failures are more frequent and complex than the frontier model but do not reach the systemic instability seen in the 120B open weights model.

The significance of this finding is that a higher success rate is often accompanied by isolated failure. Systems that fail with fewer simultaneous problems are far more predictable and simpler to improve through targeted engineering interventions.

Perhaps the most critical insight from MAST is distinguishing between failures that the system can tolerate versus those that are fatal to success of the downstream task. By comparing the distribution of failure modes in Successful Traces vs. Failed Traces, we can classify them into three categories.

Across all three models, certain failure modes appear frequently even in runs that ultimately succeed. These are often structural frictions rather than terminal bugs.

This separation is where MAST proves its value. It allows us to ignore the bening failures like repetition that often occurs in troubleshooting, and focus instead on fatal failures that killed a run.

Certain behaviors strongly separate success from failure. When these modes appear, the probability of a successful outcome drops precipitously. The most prominent example is FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification). This mode shows a 52 percent increase in failed Gemini-3-Flash traces compared to its successful ones. Other prominent failure modes are 1.5 (Unaware of Termination Conditions) and 2.6 (Reasoning Action Mismatch).

If these happen, the run is likely dead; guiding practitioners to develop robust context management strategies across agents in the system and multiple turns of interactions.

Gemini-3-Flash is highly efficient, but its primary bottleneck is its tendency to assume success without rigorous proof. Its failure signature is dominated by a massive delta in verification errors. It often identifies the correct signals but terminates before cross-referencing them against the ground truth. To fix this, developers should implement an external verification gate. By requiring tool-based evidence like a cleared alert or a healthy metric threshold before allowing the agent to exit, we can mitigate this model’s inherent overconfidence.

While termination confusion (FM-3.1 and FM-1.5) is the prevalent failure mode for Kimi-K2, its failed trajectories are defined by a pervasive Action-Reasoning Mismatch (FM-2.6), which is present in a staggering 92% of its failures.

Kimi-K2 is a good example of an overthinking model, its reasoning chains are often too long but can fail at execution.

GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the most unstable failure signature of the cohort. This model exhibits an average of 5.3 distinct failure modes per failed trace, indicating a fundamental inability to maintain internal state.

In summary, MAST lets you split failure modes into two buckets:

These are failures which are not fatal and from which the system can recover to successfully complete the task.

These are failures from which the system typically cannot recover.

This is the “richer understanding” piece: two models can have the same success rate on a small slice, yet fail for entirely different reasons—requiring different fixes.

MAST is a tool that inspects the agentic system traces to identify fine-grain failure types that support system development and debugging. In this blog, we show that by applying MAST to ITBench, we move from generic observations ("Open models struggle") to a concrete engineering roadmap that help improving the performance of agentic systems relying on thse models, e.g.:

Develop and run interactive code notebooks with JupyterLab

Develop and run interactive code notebooks with JupyterLab

#10169. AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Big US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

As governments scramble to make AI safer, who gets to write the rules could be just as important as what they say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more.

First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The company launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra.

But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI said Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want.

It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve.

For years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do.

OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here.

Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments.

Against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview.

But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO. "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.”

Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months.

That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a company’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics.

In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium, referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price.

Loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said.

She believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate.

But open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified, third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” said Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium. Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations.

Those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too.

Von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he said.

Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun said.

Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems.

For von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents.

The opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants.

Even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the company. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she said.

Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows.

There are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” said von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it."

Chris Stokel-Walker is a Tom's Hardware contributor who focuses on the tech sector and its impact on our daily lives— online and offline. He is the author of How AI Ate the World, published in 2024, as well as TikTok Boom, YouTubers, and The History of the Internet in Byte-Sized Chunks.

#10167. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Nvidia's board reportedly isn't considering Huang's return.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia who resigned last week amid the fallout from two extramarital affairs, said in his first public statement since abdicating his position that he would be willing to return to the corner office at the company he co-founded."Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement posted on X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. JensenNovember 17, 2026

Huang has seen public support from other tech founders and CEOs, such as SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. They and some investors and Nvidia employees signed an online petition and have continued to be vocal on social media, namely Musk's X. President Donald Trump also said that he "would not mind" Huang's return.Huang resigned on Thursday following two scandals: one affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed believed by some US Intelligence officials to be a potential Chinese government asset; and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and Huang's direct report.Despite Huang's apparent willingness to return, Nvidia's board doesn't seem likely to make that move. Reports yesterday claim that the board is more focused on its ongoing investigation into Huang's affairs and a national security inquiry and is not considering Huang's return. The board has also put together its own National Security and Export Control Oversight to provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.In his post on X, Huang further apologized, writing that "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation."

#10163. Jensen’s exit could be Google’s TPU moment

Good morning. Today I’m rewatching Tenet to better picture Robert Pattinson in his new role, sighing over the inevitability of delivery drones triggering PTSD symptoms, and laugh-cringing at some of these Bit.ly link hijack stories from the weekend. Plus, prayers to anyone who had to find a last-minute hotel room during last week’s flying nightmare.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the company’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has announced it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the company describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

Over the past few days, the one-two punch of Microsoft’s 365/Exchange outage and the FAA’s ground stop shows just how vulnerable everyone is to the effects of seemingly brittle tech infrastructure.

The FAA describes a flood of connection attempts that destabilized its telecommunications network, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in Arkansas and Texas that were undergoing router and wire replacements, but even days after the stop was lifted, there’s still no clear underlying cause.

Meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Microsoft says that a “latent defect” introduced into its network code in a July update wasn’t triggered until a few days ago, when high loads led to cascading failures across the company’s servers worldwide.

While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

Finally, if you’re into DIY projects, you’ve likely heard of TRMNL, the company that makes very cool and slightly overpriced ePaper displays that can be programmed to do basically whatever you want with them.

Now, the company has just revealed a 31.5-inch color ePaper version, encased in a custom wood frame, that sells for nearly $2,000. It can be mounted on a wall without internet, using a microSD card and a 20,000mAh battery, for months of gorgeous art displays, or kept powered and connected to the internet to be used as a (very large) home dashboard.

I want one very badly, but I’ve already chosen my $2,000 poison.

Vera can speed up old code out of the box, but there's more performance to unlock

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia's Vera CPU, designed as both a standalone data-center part and a host for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 servers, offers impressive performance thanks to substantially higher execution resources per core than its predecessor, Grace. However, Nvidia admits at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) that existing software cannot always take full advantage of Vera's resources without adaptation for the architecture.

The company shared that architecture-specific software optimizations can boost Vera's performance by nearly 39% in certain computationally intensive workloads. But despite offering unbeatable single-thread performance, the CPU is not positioned for general-purpose workloads.

Get the full Tom's Hardware experience on your device with our brand-new app. Bookmark articles, use our smart search feature, personalize your feed, and get push notifications so you never miss a beat.

Unlike Grace, which relies on off-the-shelf Neoverse V2 CPU cores developed by Arm, Vera uses Nvidia's proprietary Olympus cores specifically designed to maximize per-core performance as well as to ensure high aggregate throughput. To that end, Nvidia equipped Olympus with a wide front end that features a 10-wide decoder, a neural branch predictor, a deep out-of-order execution engine, six vector execution units, four load pipelines, two store pipelines, all backed with large private caches and advanced prefetch mechanisms.

In fact, Nvidia deliberately opted for 88 high-performance general-purpose cores with support for its proprietary spatial multithreading technology (176 threads in total) rather than maximizing the number of cores per socket, as the maximum possible single-thread performance was one of the key design goals for Vera.

"CPU design is really just a game of trade-offs," said Hannah Coutand, who leads Vera CPU marketing at Nvidia, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "You could maximize for a lot of cores, but literally when you maximize the die for lots of cores, you do not actually have space to maximize for IPC, like instructions per clock."

Although Nvidia primarily positions Vera as a CPU for agentic AI and other AI-related workloads, the company originally conceived its Olympus microarchitecture with data processing applications in mind. As it turned out, the key attributes of Vera — high per-core performance, high memory bandwidth, and low memory access latency — are precisely what agentic AI workloads need as well, according to Coutand.

"We are very clear in our strategy with Vera and our positioning with Vera that it is not a general-purpose CPU," Coutand said. " If you want a web server for your cloud data center, there are probably other choices that are better suited for that than Vera. [Vera is made for] workloads […] that require that high per-core speed, high memory bandwidth, low latency. […] It has great fungibility for lots of workloads as long as those workloads value the things that Vera is good for."

To assess the computational capabilities of Nvidia's custom Olympus microarchitecture and its advantages over Neoverse V2, Nvidia's researchers used a double-precision general matrix multiplication (DGEMM) workload based on an assembly kernel from OpenBLAS, an open-source linear algebra library. While OpenBLAS features a kernel tailored for the Arm Neoverse V2 cores that power Nvidia's Grace processor, it lacks one specifically designed for Olympus.

To examine the efficiency of the two microarchitectures, the researchers used a standalone benchmark called miniKernelGEMM with a 128 × 128 matrix multiplication problem that fits into the L1 cache of both processors.

The Grace CPU achieved 4.51 instructions per clock (IPC) and 13.03 FP64 operations per cycle with the Neoverse V2 kernel, whereas Vera executed 5.43 instructions per clock and 15.69 FP64 operations per cycle with the very same code, an improvement of approximately 20%.

However, when the researchers used a kernel specifically optimized for Olympus, Vera’s performance increased to 7.53 instructions per clock and 21.75 FP64 operations per cycle. As a result, Vera outperformed its predecessor by nearly 67% on a per-core, per-clock basis in this particular workload.

Grace's Neoverse V2 microarchitecture has four 128-bit SIMD pipelines that can perform a total of 16 FP64 operations per clock, whereas Nvidia's Olympus has six such pipelines that can execute up to 24 FP64 operations per cycle, a 50% improvement.

But where the Neoverse V2-optimized kernel uses 81.4% of Grace's peak FP64 throughput, it uses only about 66.5% of Vera's computational capabilities. With changes to matrix tile organization, register allocation, and instruction scheduling that better suit the Olympus microarchitecture, the researchers managed to utilize 90.6% of its peak FP64 throughput, according to Nvidia's tutorial published at SC26.

While software developed and optimized for existing Arm-based data center processors can still benefit from the capabilities of Nvidia's Olympus cores without any specific optimizations, the company's SC26 benchmark results demonstrate that at least some applications will need to be fine-tuned for the new microarchitecture to take full advantage of its execution resources. Of course, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained through Olympus-specific optimizations in workloads other than matrix multiplication.

As Nvidia expands beyond CPUs that primarily serve as companions to its data center GPUs and chases the standalone server CPU market, the company will have to ensure that performance-critical software takes advantage of the architectural peculiarities of its processors, much like Intel and AMD have done for decades.

But the company is already deeply experienced with partner and ecosystem development for platforms like CUDA, so as Vera is more widely adopted, that experience could prove useful in spurring optimizations for these CPUs going forward.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

#10160. Google’s new ‘Fast Switch’ feature leaks, lets you use one number on two Android phones

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

#10159. Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit.

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.
