Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

#10132. You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a new one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.)

Email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”

#10131. Introducing Storage Buckets on the Hugging Face Hub

Hugging Face Models and Datasets repos are great for publishing final artifacts. But production ML generates a constant stream of intermediate files (checkpoints, optimizer states, processed shards, logs, traces, etc.) that change often, arrive from many jobs at once, and rarely need version control.

Storage Buckets are built exactly for this: mutable, S3-like object storage you can browse on the Hub, script from Python, or manage with the hf CLI. And because they are backed by Xet, they are especially efficient for ML artifacts that share content across files.

Git starts to feel like the wrong abstraction pretty quickly when you're dealing with:

The storage need in all these cases is the same: write fast, overwrite when needed, sync directories, remove stale files, and keep things moving.

A Bucket is a non-versioned storage container on the Hub. It lives under a user or organization namespace, has standard Hugging Face permissions, can be private or public, has a page you can open in your browser, and can be addressed programmatically with a handle like hf://buckets/username/my-training-bucket.

Buckets are built on Xet, Hugging Face’s chunk-based storage backend, and this matters more than it might seem.

Instead of treating files as monolithic blobs, Xet breaks content into chunks and deduplicates across them. Upload a processed dataset that’s mostly similar to the raw one? Many chunks already exist. Store successive checkpoints where large parts of the model are frozen? Same story. Buckets skip the bytes that are already there, which means less bandwidth, faster transfers, and more efficient storage.

This is a natural fit for ML workloads. Training pipelines constantly produce families of related artifacts — raw and processed data, successive checkpoints, Agent traces and derived summaries — and Xet is designed to take advantage of that overlap.

For Enterprise customers, billing is based on deduplicated storage, so shared chunks directly reduce the billed footprint. Deduplication helps with both speed and cost.

Buckets live on the Hub, which means global storage by default. But not every workload can afford to pull data from wherever it happens to live, for distributed training and large-scale pipelines, storage location directly affects throughput.

Pre-warming lets you bring hot data closer to the cloud provider and region where your compute runs. Instead of data traveling across regions on every read, you declare where you need it and Buckets make sure it's already there when your jobs start. This is especially useful for training clusters that need fast access to large datasets or checkpoints, and for multi-region setups where different parts of a pipeline run in different clouds.

We are partnering with AWS and GCP to start with, more more cloud providers coming in the future.

You can get a bucket up and running in under 2 minutes with the hf CLI. First thing is to install it and log in:

Say your training job is writing checkpoints locally to ./checkpoints. Sync that directory into the Bucket:

For large transfers, you might want to see what will happen before anything moves. --dry-run prints the plan without executing anything:

You can also save the plan to a file for review and apply it later:

Once done, inspect the Bucket from the CLI:

or browse it directly on the Hub at https://huggingface.co/buckets/username/my-training-bucket.

That is the whole loop. Create a bucket, sync your working data into it, check on it when you need to, and save the versioned repo for when something is worth publishing. For one-off operations, hf buckets cp copies individual files and hf buckets remove cleans up stale objects.

Everything above also works from Python via huggingface_hub (available since v1.5.0). The API follows the same pattern: create, sync, inspect.

This makes it straightforward to integrate Buckets into training scripts, data pipelines, or any service that manages artifacts programmatically. The Python client also supports batch uploads, selective downloads, deletes, and bucket moves for when you need finer control.

Bucket support is also available in JavaScript via @huggingface/hub (since v2.10.5), so you can integrate Buckets into Node.js services and web applications as well.

Buckets also work through HfFileSystem, the fsspec-compatible filesystem in huggingface_hub. This means you can list, read, write, and glob Bucket contents using standard filesystem operations — and any library that supports fsspec can access Buckets directly.

Because fsspec is the standard Python interface for remote filesystems, libraries like pandas, Polars, and Dask can read from and write to Buckets using hf:// paths with no extra setup:

This makes it easy to plug Buckets into existing data workflows without changing how your code reads or writes files.

Buckets are the fast, mutable place where artifacts live while they are still in motion. Once something becomes a stable deliverable, it usually belongs to a versioned model or dataset repo.

On the roadmap, we plan to support direct transfers between Buckets and repos in both directions: promote final checkpoint weights into a model repo, or commit processed shards into a dataset repo once a pipeline completes. The working layer and the publishing layer stay separate, but fit into one continuous Hub-native workflow.

Before opening Buckets to everyone, we ran a private beta with a small group of launch partners.

A huge thank you to Jasper, Arcee, IBM, and PixAI for testing early versions, surfacing bugs, and sharing feedback that directly shaped this feature.

Storage Buckets bring a missing storage layer to the Hub. They give you a Hub-native place for the mutable, high-throughput side of ML: checkpoints, processed data, Agent traces, logs, and everything else that is useful before it becomes final.

Because they are built on Xet, Buckets are not just easier to use than forcing everything through Git. They are also more efficient for the kinds of related artifacts AI systems produce all the time. That means faster transfers, better deduplication, and on Enterprise plans, billing that benefits from the deduplicated footprint.

If you already use the Hub, Buckets let you keep more of your workflow in one place. If you come from S3-style storage, they give you a familiar model with better alignment to AI artifacts and a clear path toward final publication on the Hub.

Buckets are included in existing Hub storage plans. Free accounts come with storage to get started, and PRO and Enterprise plans offer higher limits. See the storage page for details.

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far."

Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

On net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

#10128. Agent Distraction

What is easy for humans to skim past in code, agents see as a call to action. They do not know better, latching on to that which is littered across the files read during the planning and research phase of the coding journey.

As agents' agency through tools and skills grows the ability for side-quests scales proportionally. Obsolete specs, long resolved bugs, and lagging documentation no longer rest in long forgotten corners of the codebase, but rather are unintentionally ingested as context indirecting and misdirecting the next wave of coders - the agents. This indirection is not free: in the best case it only costs tokens, steps, and time - in the worst case it distracts and grounds the agent on falsehoods leading to incorrect logic and decisions during implementation.

Measuring how often agents fall into these traps across millions of monthly sessions is impossible with manual human review - we need an objective signal derivable from the code itself. Inline TODO(bug/...) comments provide the perfect proxy. TODOs tend to be left behind long after the underlying bug is resolved or abandoned, while the linked bug ticket acts as the canonical record. By cross-referencing every TODO an agent encounters against the TODO's bug status and the user's prompt, we can automatically separate valid work from wasted detours at scale.

By leveraging the distributed traces of agent interactions across thousands of engineers and over hundreds of millions of individual agent steps, we quantify the impact of TODO distractions in the codebase and how agents act on them:

Controlling for developer, codebase complexity, task type, model tier, number of files read, initial prompt length, and the step where the bug reference appeared, using a multi-way fixed-effects regression with developer-clustered standard errors, we see that unprompted bug detours add substantial overhead (all stat sig p<0.0001). Per session:

The Obsolete Detour: In the following trajectory we can observe how this drift plays out. During an investigation into an unrelated bug The agent views SurfaceControlTest.java and sees // TODO(bug/XXX)

This bug, while fixed in 2023, remains lingering in the codebase leading to subsequent investigation distraction across Steps with the agent digging into the bug to learn more.

The Eager Agent: In the trajectory the agent encountered a TODO in the bug it was investigating and decided (unprompted) to "fix" the code

The agent executed multiple Code Search and internal knowledge search queries for the bug ultimately resulting in the agent changing the ModelDownloaderV1 code. Later in the trajectory the human challenged the scope creep.

With the model when admitting it was an incorrect increase in scope:

While in both of these cases they were only trivial to minor detours - they were real distractions costing time, tokens, and human intervention.

As part of addressing this finding at scale we created agents that scrubbed the totality of our codebases, finding bug references in the code that were marked as fixed or obsolete for cleanup. That step alone however was not enough to determine if the TODOs in the codebase were load-bearing or not. The agents had to go further looking at the history of the bug, the file, and changes to the codebase, at times spanning years of history. Only in cases where the agent was able to confirm that the TODO and the intent behind the TODO was obsolete did our agent send a change for review to delete it from the codebase. As a result of this multi-layer approach, our todo cleaner has been able to remove thousands of actually obsolete references over the last 6 months exceeding 95% acceptance from human reviewers.

In recap, as we task agents on more and more ambitious problems, "agent friendly codebases" require more than just the code in the hotpath being healthy. The forgotten corners of the codebase now more than ever carry a significant tax levied against agents.

Tooling like presubmit analyzers, entire corpus scanners, and automated coding agents to remediate dead-todos offer out of the box ready to scale solutions to address the tax enabling a healthier and distraction free codebase for agents to thrive.

Projects that once were on the backburner to cleanup lingering debt but deprioritized due to perceived low value need to be reevaluated with the new agents acting at scale on your codebase.

#10126. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

#10124. Holotron-12B - High Throughput Computer Use Agent

We're thrilled to release Holotron-12B, a multimodal computer-use model from H Company. Post-trained from the open NVIDIA Nemotron-Nano-2 VL model on H Company’s proprietary data mixture, Holotron-12B is the result of a close collaboration between our research labs to engineer a new type of model optimized primarily for scale and performance in production.

H Company is part of the NVIDIA Inception Program.

The model is now available on Hugging Face.

Most multimodal models today optimize primarily for static vision or following instructions. Holotron-12B, just like our Holo2 model, however, has a different goal: serving as a policy model for computer-use agents that must perceive, decide, and act efficiently in interactive environments.

With Holotron-12B, we wanted to create a model that could efficiently and effectively scale in production while handling long contexts with multiple images, and still perform well on agent benchmarks. The NVIDIA Nemotron model offered a strong foundation on the inference side, and by developing Holotron-12B we've demonstrated how much more the model can accomplish with further training.

Holotron-12B's significant leap in inference efficiency is made possible by its foundational Nemotron architecture, which utilizes a hybrid State-Space Model (SSM) and attention mechanism. Unlike purely transformer-based models, this design is optimized for high-throughput serving. State-space models offer superior scalability for long-context inference by avoiding the quadratic computation cost associated with the full attention mechanism, particularly benefiting agentic workloads involving multiple images and lengthy interaction histories. In terms of inference, the main contribution of an SSM is its dramatically reduced memory-footprint: while vanilla attention stores K and V activations per token and layer (the notorious KV Cache), SSMs are a linear recurrent model, storing only a constant state per layer per generated sequence, independent of the length of the sequence.

When evaluated on the WebVoyager Benchmark, the model excels using a real-world multimodal agentic workload featuring long context, multiple high-resolution images, and a high request concurrency of 100 benchmark workers. Running on a single H100 GPU and using vLLM with the latest SSM optimizations (v0.14.1), Holotron-12B achieved an over 2x higher throughput compared to Holo2-8B. This makes Holotron-12B an attractive choice for throughput-bound workloads, such as data generation, annotation, and online reinforcement learning.

In a controlled experiment setup (see figure 2), Holotron-12B continues to scale efficiently as concurrency increases, with total token throughput rising steadily to 8.9k tokens/s at a max concurrency of 100. In contrast, the total token throughput of Holo2-8B plateaus much more quickly at 5.1k tokens/s. This behaviour highlights a key strength of the Nemotron architecture, namely more effective and efficient VRAM utilization, and smaller overall memory footprint, which allows much larger effective batch sizes on the same hardware. Even at large batch sizes, Holotron-12B maintains strong throughput.

Holotron-12B was trained in two stages. We started from Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2-VL-BF16, a multimodal base model published by NVIDIA. We then performed supervised fine-tuning on H Company’s proprietary localization and navigation data mixture, focusing on screen understanding, grounding, and UI-level interactions.

The final checkpoint was trained on approximately 14 billion tokens.

On computer-use and navigation benchmarks, Holotron-12B shows strong improvements over the Nemotron base model and strong performance with established agent models. Its WebVoyager performance increased from 35.1% to 80.5%, exceeding Holo2-8B’s performance on the benchmark and illustrating the model’s ability to perform effectively in an agentic setting.

Holotron-12B also improves substantially over the base Nemotron model on localization and grounding benchmarks such as OS-World-G, GroundUI, and WebClick.

Holotron-12B demonstrates that the NVIDIA Nemotron VL model provides a strong foundation for real-world multimodal agents when paired with the right training setup and infrastructure work.

The model offers strong agent performance, significantly improved inference throughput, and a clear path for future improvements, particularly around higher-resolution vision training.

We look forward to seeing what others build with Holotron-12B. The model and checkpoints are available now on Hugging Face under an NVIDIA Open Model License.

NVIDIA announced today the release of Nemotron 3 Omni. Building on the success of Holotron-12B, we are preparing to post-train this next generation of multimodal models. By leveraging the enhanced hybrid SSM-Attention and MoE architectural foundations of the Nemotron 3 family, we aim to deliver even greater leaps in reasoning capabilities and multimodal precision with the newly announced Nemotron 3 Omni. As this evolution pushes Holotron beyond research and into a commercial application, it will provide enterprises with the high-throughput, low-latency performance required for massive-scale autonomous "computer use" deployments.

#10121. State of Open Source on Hugging Face: Spring 2026

This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year. We primarily examine community activity on Hugging Face across many types of metrics to give a holistic view of the ecosystem.

This post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, available here, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building. We recommend reading additional perspectives on the open source ecosystem in and outside of Hugging Face from the Data Provenance Initiative, Interconnects, OpenRouter and a16z, and MIT and the Linux Foundation. As the Hugging Face ecosystem is distributed, analyses are a combination of Hugging Face and community members' work, each of which is appropriately credited.

Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of users, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling. In 2025, Hugging Face grew to 13 million users, more than 2 million public models, and over 500,000 public datasets. This growth signals more than increased interest in open source; it reflects a shift toward active participation, with users increasingly creating derivative artifacts such as fine-tuned models, adapters, benchmarks, and applications rather than only consuming pre-trained systems.

Data from Hugging Face | Hugging Face's two million models and counting: Graph and story by AI World

The ecosystem remains highly concentrated. Approximately half of the models on Hugging Face have less than 200 total downloads, and the top 200 most downloaded models, or 0.01% of models, comprise 49.6% of all downloads.

Specialized communities form around particular domains, languages, or problem areas, and often show sustained engagement and reuse even when their overall download counts are modest. Open source AI is best understood as a collection of overlapping sub-ecosystems rather than a single uniform market.

More companies, both large and small, are building on open source. Over 30% of the Fortune 500 now maintain verified accounts on Hugging Face. Startups frequently use open models as default components: Thinking Machines built its Tinker model options entirely on open weights, while popular IDEs such as VSCode and Cursor support both open and closed models. Established American companies such as Airbnb have increased their engagement with the open ecosystem, and Hugging Face has seen more legacy companies upgrading their organizational subscriptions over the course of 2025.

Big Tech companies are frequently creating new repositories on Hugging Face Hub; visualized side-by-side, the strong increase in repository growth shows investment over time. NVIDIA has emerged as the strongest contributor.

Data from Hugging Face | Big Tech Is All-In On Open-Source AI, Graph and story by AI World

Studies of open software more broadly suggest that the downstream value created by open artifacts far exceeds the cost of producing them. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, where open models are reused, adapted, and specialized across thousands of downstream applications. Organizations that rely exclusively on closed systems often incur higher costs and face reduced flexibility in deployment and customization.

All-time downloads over the past four years show clear frontrunner regions in model popularity. The U.S. and China have historically been top contributors, with the UK, Germany, and France as secondary in popularity. Models developed by individual users or distributed organizations without a clear geographic base account for about half of all platform downloads.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

The geographic composition of the open source ecosystem has fundamentally changed. Hugging Face data shows China surpassing the U.S. in monthly downloads and overall downloads. In the past year, Chinese models quickly accounted for the plurality or 41% of downloads.

Industry's share of overall development fell from around 70% before 2022 to roughly 37% in 2025. Meanwhile, independent or unaffiliated developers rose from 17% to 39% of all downloads over the same period, at times accounting for more than half of total usage. Individuals and small collectives focused on quantizing, adapting, and redistributing base models. These intermediaries now steer a meaningful portion of what typical users can run and how innovations spread through the ecosystem.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

Different regions contribute in different ways. The United States and Western Europe have historically dominated through large industry labs (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Stability AI), while China has increasingly led on both releases and adoption. France, Germany, and the UK continue to contribute through research organizations, national AI initiatives, and specialized model families. Ecosystems supporting a variety of contributors and organizational forms tend to produce more widely adopted artifacts.

Popular models from startups were more widespread. Competitive countries were France and South Korea. Notably, the fourth most popular entity for developing new trending models were individual users, not organizations. Creating competitive models at a user level is more accessible than ever before.

Of the newly created models in 2025, the majority of trending models were either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China. The most popular models were developed by large organizations, predominantly from the U.S. and China. For more on the Chinese AI ecosystem, read our three part series reflecting on the changes in one year since the "DeepSeek Moment", with one on strategic changes, two on architectural changes, and three on organizations and the future.

In 2025, China’s AI ecosystem steered heavily into open source, following the viral release of DeepSeek’s R1 model in January. The number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing models and the number of repositories on Hugging Face skyrocketed. Baidu went from zero releases on the Hub in 2024 to over 100 in 2025. ByteDance and Tencent each increased releases by eight to nine times. Organizations that had previously favored closed approaches, including Baidu and MiniMax, shifted decisively toward open releases.

A similar number of popular U.S. organizations have consistently contributed a higher volume of repositories over time. Meta and its former Facebook research organization account for a significant proportion of open releases, as does Google to a lesser extent.

Next to each other, the steep upward trajectory of repository growth among popular Chinese organizations emerges as a key strategic difference.

Open source AI is increasingly tied to questions of sovereignty. Open weight models allow governments and public institutions to fine-tune systems on local data under national legal frameworks. Models that can be deployed on domestic hardware reduce reliance on foreign-controlled cloud infrastructure. Transparency around model architecture, training processes, and evaluation supports regulatory review and public accountability. Read more about the open source approach to sovereignty here.

At the national level, governments are taking action. South Korea's National Sovereign AI Initiative launched mid-2025 named national champions LG AI Research, SK Telecom, Naver Cloud, NC AI, and Upstage to produce competitive domestic models. Three models from South Korea trended simultaneously on Hugging Face Hub in February 2026. In March 2026, In 2026, South Korea and U.S. startup Reflection AI announced a data center partnership, also bringing frontier open weight models to South Korea.

Switzerland's Swiss AI initiative and various EU-funded projects reflect similar priorities. The UK's principle of "public money, public code" has influenced several government-backed AI initiatives.

These investments in open-source and open weight AI are already paying dividends for countries with thriving AI training ecosystems of their own, as we see that models and datasets are typically most used in the regions where they're developed; with developers often turning to the models that best represent their languages and reflect similar technical and application requirements.

Most liked models on the Hub show community attention, in terms of ability to go back to or reference the model or general popularity. While this metric does not always reflect usage, the attention collected over time can show signals of interest. In one year, the most liked models went from predominantly U.S.-developed from Meta’s Llama family, to an international mix with China’s DeepSeek-R1 at the top.

While determining the value of scientific contributions can be determined by many metrics, our upvote feature on the Hub shows papers from large AI organizations be widely appreciated by community members. Notably, the most upvoted papers are from large organizations, mostly from the U.S. and China. The majority of the top organizations are Chinese Big Tech companies, with ByteDance sharing a high volume of high impact papers.

Space by Hugging Face | PaperVerse Explorer

Of Hugging Face's Daily Papers, a set of papers curated by Hugging Face's AK, papers that reference model and dataset creation, showing the most open source adoption, are generally diverse. Prominent takeaways show medical papers being influential, while Big Tech's influence is sparse.

Data from Hugging Face | Graphic and story by AI World

How our community members choose to build on models, whether via fine-tuning, merging, or other methods, reflects model popularity and usability. Alibaba as an organization has more derivative models than both Google and Meta combined, with the Qwen family constituting more than 113,000 derivative models. When including all models that tag Qwen, that number balloons to over 200,000 models.

Model development has increasingly emphasized accessibility alongside scale. Smaller models are downloaded and deployed at far higher rates than very large systems, reflecting practical constraints around cost, latency, and hardware availability.

This small-model dominance occurs in part because far more models are released at that size. But even when normalizing for this, the data from the ATOM Project's Relative Adoption Metric shows that the median top-10 models from 1-9B parameters are only downloaded about 4x more than models above 100B. Automated systems and CI pipelines further inflate small model download counts, but the trend toward smaller, deployable models is real.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Article by ATOM

Engagement with open models tends to peak almost immediately after release, then slow. Mean engagement duration is approximately 6 weeks. Continuous improvement and frequent updates have become critical for maintaining relevance. DeepSeek's successive releases (V3, R1, V3.2) kept it competitive even as challengers emerged. Organizations that stagnate in development tend to lose share quickly to those with frequent updates or domain-specific fine-tunes.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Choksi et al. "The Brief and Wondrous Life of Open Models"

The mean size of downloaded open models rose from 827M parameters in 2023 to 20.8B in 2025, driven largely by quantization and mixture-of-experts architectures. The median, however, increased only marginally, from 326M to 406M parameters. This divergence indicates that high-end LLM users are pulling up the mean while underlying small-model usage remains stable.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. "Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem"

Performance differences between frontier models and smaller systems often narrow rapidly through fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation. On the Hub, models with hundreds of millions of parameters support search, tagging, and document processing workflows, while models in the single-digit billions are widely used for coding, reasoning, and multimodal tasks. As a result, most major model developers now release families of models spanning a range of sizes. The rise of capable small models shifts autonomy closer to the edge, reducing dependency on centralized cloud providers.

Open source AI development is closely linked to hardware trends. Most models are optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, but support for AMD hardware continues to expand. Stability AI model collections now optimize for both NVIDIA and AMD platforms. Libraries increasingly target both, and tooling has improved to make cross-hardware deployment more straightforward. In 2025 Hugging Face launched the Kernel Hub to load and run kernels optimized for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

In parallel, Chinese open models are being released with explicit support for domestically developed chips. Alibaba has invested in inference-focused chip architectures designed to fill Chinese data centers with hardware capable of running open source models locally.

While access to compute remains a core necessity across the board for development and deployment of AI models, open-source and open-weight models are helping break away from an ecosystem where it becomes the be-all and end-all, with increasingly more models at all levels of performance pushing efficiency from 10x to 1000x lower costs than flagship AI models the largest developers.

Still, the question of infrastructure investment for open source remains urgent. Public funding for data centers capable of training and serving open models has become a growing policy discussion, particularly in Europe and the UK. The gap between the compute resources available to large closed-model companies and those accessible to the open source community continues to shape what is feasible in open development.

Robotics has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sub-communities on Hugging Face. The numbers are striking: robotics datasets grew from 1,145 in 2024 to 26,991 in 2025, climbing from rank 44 to the single largest dataset category on the Hub in just three years. For comparison, text generation, the second-largest category, had only around 5,000 datasets in 2025.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Story by AI World

Community-contributed datasets span everything from household manipulation tasks to autonomous driving. The largest multimodal dataset for spatial intelligence, Learning to Drive (L2D), was released through a LeRobot collaboration with Yaak. Datasets like RoboMIND, with over 107,000 real-world trajectories across 479 distinct tasks and multiple robot embodiments, provide the kind of scale and diversity needed for training generalizable robotic policies.

Hugging Face's acquisition of Pollen Robotics opened open source robotic sales to both industry and academic labs, as well as everyday hobbyists. LeRobot, Hugging Face's open source robotics library that provides models, datasets, and tools for real-world robotics in PyTorch, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and vision-language-action models, experienced rapid growth. Over the past year, its GitHub repository stars nearly tripled.

Data from GitHub | Graphic from star-history.com

Scientific research has become another particularly active area. Open models and datasets are increasingly used for protein folding, molecular dynamics, drug discovery, and scientific data analysis. All frontier AI companies now have dedicated science teams, though much current focus remains on literature discovery rather than direct experimentation.

Space by Hugging Face | Science Release Heatmap

Community-led projects have formed around shared research goals, often involving hundreds of contributors working across institutions and disciplines. These efforts highlight the role of open source as a mechanism for coordinating large-scale, interdisciplinary work that would be difficult to organize through traditional academic or corporate structures alone.

The open source AI ecosystem continues to evolve through a combination of global participation, technical specialization, and institutional adoption. Several trends are likely to define the next phase.

The geographic rebalancing of power is accelerating. Western organizations increasingly seek commercially deployable alternatives to Chinese models, creating urgency around efforts like OpenAI's GPT-OSS, AI2's OLMo, and Google's Gemma to offer competitive open options from US and European developers. Whether these efforts can match the adoption momentum of Qwen and DeepSeek will be a defining question of 2026.

The growth of sub-communities in robotics and science suggests that open source AI is expanding beyond language and image generation into the physical and experimental domains. The infrastructure, norms, and coordination mechanisms developed around text and image models are being adapted for new modalities and use cases.

For researchers, developers, companies, and governments, open source remains a foundational layer for building, evaluating, and governing AI systems. With increasing agent deployments, open-source and its interoperability will be key for agents to thrive. Its trajectory over the past year makes one thing clear: the open source ecosystem is where much of the practical work of AI development, adaptation, and deployment takes place, and its influence on the broader AI landscape continues to grow.

Thank you to the Hugging Face community for continuing to build the foundation of the AI ecosystem 🤗

#10119. WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

#10118. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

#10117. Build a Domain-Specific Embedding Model in Under a Day

If you are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system, you have likely hit this wall: Everything works… until it doesn’t. General-purpose embedding models are trained to understand the internet; not your contracts, manufacturing logs, proprietary chemical formulations or internal taxonomy. They capture broad semantic similarity, but they do not understand the fine-grained distinctions that matter in your domain. Fine-tuning an embedding model can improve the performance of your retrieval pipeline when off-the-shelf models fail to effectively capture domain-specific nuances. Despite how critical embeddings are to RAG performance, the process remains surprisingly fragmented, the skills required are specialized, and the time investment is daunting.

With a single GPU and less than a day of training time, you can transform a general-purpose embedding model into one that truly understands your domain, no manual labeling required. To help you hit the ground running, we are also releasing a ready-to-use synthetic training dataset generated from NVIDIA's public documentation using this exact pipeline. Using this data and the recipe, we saw over 10% improvement in both Recall@10 and NDCG@10. Atlassian applied this recipe to fine-tune on their JIRA dataset, increasing Recall@60 from 0.751 to 0.951, a 26% improvement - on a single GPU.

By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:📄 Generate training data from domain documents without labeled data🎯 Use hard negative mining for effective contrastive training🔗 Improve embedding quality with multi-hop queries⚙️ Fine-tune a bi-encoder embedding model📊 Evaluate whether fine-tuning improves retrieval🚀 Deploy the fine-tuned model in your pipeline

In this tutorial, we will finetune the base model Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 - a 1-billion-parameter embedding model that balances quality and inference cost. To get started, follow this setup guide.

Fine-tuning an embedding model requires thousands of (query, relevant document) pairs. Most use cases don’t have this data readily available. Creating it manually is expensive, slow, and often biased by the annotator’s personal interpretation of what’s “relevant.”Instead of labeling data by hand, you can use an LLM (nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b) to read your documents and automatically generate high-quality synthetic question–answer pairs.

Behind the scenes, this runs a four-stage synthetic data generation (SDG) pipeline powered by NeMo Data Designer:

The thermal design power (TDP) of the H100 GPU is 700W in SXM form factor. The cooling solution must maintain junction temperature below 83°C under sustained workloads. Liquid cooling is recommended for dense deployments exceeding 4 GPUs per node, as air cooling cannot dissipate sufficient heat in standard 2U chassis configurations.

Notice the difference: the first question is a simple factual lookup. The second requires multi-hop, causal reasoning. The pipeline generates both types, with configurable complexity levels (2–5) and hop counts (1–3). Each QA pair then undergoes quality evaluation, receiving sub-scores for relevance, accuracy, context support, and clarity, along with an overall score. Only pairs that meet the threshold are included in training.

If you train an embedding model with only positive pairs (query + correct document), it learns to distinguish obviously different documents but fails on the hard cases — passages that look relevant but are not the right answer. In a real retrieval system, these near-misses are exactly the documents that cause bad answers. Hard negative mining finds these confusing passages so the model can learn to tell them apart.

The above command runs three sub-steps automatically:

The generated QA pairs are split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The test set is formatted as a BEIR-compatible benchmark for standardized evaluation in Step 5.

Using the base embedding model, the pipeline:

The result: hard negatives are the most similar non-positive passages that still fall safely below the positive-score ceiling. They are passages the current model considers highly relevant but that are not the labeled answer.

Why this works: Training on easy negatives (completely unrelated passages) teaches the model nothing new. Training on hard negatives forces it to learn the subtle distinctions that matter in your domain. For example, in a medical corpus, a question about "metformin dosage for Type 2 diabetes" might have hard negatives about "metformin side effects" or "insulin dosage for Type 1 diabetes" — close but critically different. The 95% margin ceiling prevents the miner from selecting passages that are too close to the positive, which could actually be correct answers that simply weren't labeled during SDG.

Multi-hop questions reference multiple positive documents. For example, a question like "How does the thermal management system in Section 3.2 relate to the power constraints described in Section 5.1?" has two positive passages.

Unrolling creates one training example per (query, positive document) pair, so the contrastive loss sees each positive independently. A question with 2 positive documents becomes 2 training examples, each with the same hard negatives but a different positive.

The final output is a training-ready JSON file:

Standard embedding fine-tuning generates one question per passage and trains the model to match them. This works for simple factual lookups, but real users ask complex questions that span multiple documents or sections. If the model has only seen single-hop training data, it will struggle to retrieve all the relevant passages for these complex queries.

The SDG pipeline generates questions at 1 to 3 hops by default:

Each hop is tracked with its own context summary and segment IDs, so the training data preserves the full reasoning chain. After unrolling (Step 2c), each (question, relevant passage) pair becomes an independent training signal, teaching the model that all of these passages are relevant to the multi-hop query.

The fine-tuned model learns to retrieve contextually related documents, not just lexically similar ones.

The training uses a biencoder architecture with contrastive loss.

The temperature of 0.02 is deliberately aggressive, it produces a very sharp probability distribution. This works well because the hard negatives from Step 2 are high-quality: they are genuinely confusing passages that the model needs strong gradients to learn to distinguish.

If ckpt_every_steps is omitted from the config, checkpoint frequency is set automatically:

This means you can start with a small corpus (50–100 documents) for a quick proof-of-concept and scale up later without manually tuning checkpoint settings.

Did fine-tuning actually help? Let’s find out by running a standardized evaluation comparing the base model against the fine-tuned checkpoint on the held-out test set:

The evaluation uses the BEIR framework and computes four standard information retrieval metrics at k = 1, 5, 10, and 100:

A successful fine-tune typically results in a 10% improvement in nDCG@10 and Recall@10 within <1 day.

Results using Retrieval Synthetic NVDocs:

This recipe has been validated on real enterprise data by Atlassian. They applied this pipeline to fine-tune Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 on a public Jira dataset using a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, following the same stages described above

Recall@60 jumped from 0.751 to 0.951 — a 26.7% gain.The fine-tuned model retrieves the correct document within the top 60 results for 95.1% of queries, up from 75.1% with the base model. For a retrieval system underpinning Jira search, this directly translates into more relevant results for millions of users. Find more details in their blog post Advancing semantic search for millions of Rovo users.

A PyTorch checkpoint is great for evaluation but too slow for production. The final two stages convert the model and serve it behind an API.

This exports the fine-tuned checkpoint to ONNX (opset 17). Optionally, it compiles a TensorRT engine for maximum inference throughput, with configurable optimization profiles for batch size (1–64) and sequence length (3–256):

The exported model is deployed inside an NVIDIA NIM container — a production-ready inference microservice exposing an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint:

Because NIM serves an OpenAI-compatible API, you can drop it into any existing RAG pipeline that uses the embeddings API format — no code changes needed.

The pipeline includes a NIM accuracy verification step that runs the same BEIR evaluation against the deployed endpoint:

This catches any accuracy loss from the ONNX/TensorRT conversion. Metrics that match within tolerance (0.03 for @1, 0.01 for @5+) are marked with a check; deviations beyond conversion noise are flagged.

The full embedding fine-tuning pipeline can be run in six commands, from raw documents to a deployed model.

Total: under a day, with most time being hands-off training. For a small corpus (~500 documents), the entire pipeline completes in about 2–3 hours.

The pipeline can run end-to-end, but each stage can also be executed independently depending on your starting point. For example, if you have raw documents, you can begin with synthetic data generation (SDG), while datasets that already include hard negatives can skip earlier steps and go directly to fine-tuning. Since every stage uses standard formats such as JSON, BEIR, and ONNX, it’s easy to integrate custom components or reuse intermediate outputs in other workflows. The recipe is also flexible in how it runs, supporting execution on a local machine, inside Docker containers, or on Slurm-based clusters.

If you have domain documents and some time in your hand, you can generate your first batch of synthetic training data today! The full pipeline - from documents to a deployed, domain-adapted embedding model - runs in under a day on a single GPU. You can start with our ready-made nvidia/Retrieval-Synthetic-NVDocs-v1 dataset to try the pipeline right away. Let us know what you build.Star the repos for Nemotron, NeMo Data Designer and NeMo Automodel if you find them useful.

Thank you Nvidia for this. Could you please make it possible, even if not the default, to call a "locally" / internally deployed LLM (OpenAI compatible endpoint) for the SDG phase ? The whole point of self-hosting a fine-tuned embedding model, appart from accurracy, is that the company's data never leave the premises. Thanks

Thanks for the feedback. We will add the support in the next release of the recipe.

The domain-specific evaluation and the thread's point about keeping sensitive data local are both important. Before choosing whether to fine-tune an embedding model, a useful control is a lexical baseline on the same held-out domain queries, including paraphrase-heavy and exact-identifier slices. We explored BM25 + semantic reranking here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). Our reranking experiment uses a hosted API, so it doesn't satisfy a strict no-data-leaves-premises requirement; we haven't compared it with this recipe.

Turns old Game Boy cartridges into a chiptune jukebox.
